human_tolerance.notes: Takes readily to bird feeders in the northern part of its range, which the article gives as one reason the species has expanded northward, and nests in bird boxes, mailboxes, sheds and other man-made cavities.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Judgement window, taken from the closest sourced regional dates: 'Egg laying dates and clutch size vary by region; in Texas the time period is from late February to late August, while in Iowa it ranges from late April to June.' Texas is the nearest region the article dates, and Arkansas sits between the two, so late February to late August is used and the day boundaries are the author's judgement.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Judgement window for the rest of the year, when 'During the winter season, males are more responsible for guarding the territory' and pairs hold a territory and roost together.

vocalizations.description: Males only, and year round 'and at any point during the daytime, except during the most harsh weather conditions', from a repertoire of 'at least twenty different phrase patterns and on average, thirty two'; transcribed as teakettle-teakettle-teakettle and cheery-cheery-cheery, with one pattern repeated for several minutes and the tail pointed downward while singing.

The alarm call, given by both sexes in territorial disputes and encounters with predators; in southern regions of the range the alarm sound is 'a ringing pink or p'dink', and only males produce the cheer call.
A paired dit-dit or chatter used only by females, 'used exclusively with territorial encounters with male song, and the song can either follow or overlap her mate's song'.

taxonomy.note: Latham 1783, Thryothorus ludovicianus; family Troglodytidae per the GBIF backbone and ITIS TSN 178581.

common_names.note: en/fr/es labels; the English name follows the Wikipedia article title, the fr/es labels the Wikidata sitelink titles.

range.note: From the lead and habitat section: 'common in the eastern United States, the extreme south of Ontario, Canada, the northeast and southeast of Mexico, and into northern Central America', with permanent breeding 'from eastern Nebraska, southern Michigan, southeast Ontario and the New England states to Mexican states such as Coahuila, Nuevo Leon, San Luis Potosi and Tamaulipas and the Gulf Coast of the United States' and occasional vagrants beyond. Koppen classes are the author's judgement of the described range.

traits.limb_count.note: Biped: two legs, the forelimbs modified as wings.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'Carolina wrens spend the majority of their time on or near the ground searching for food, or in tangles of vegetation and vines', moving with the short hops of a small wren and flying between cover; the ground walk and run the article describes are folded into the block model's hop.

traits.thermoregulation.note: Endotherm: a small bird that 'sing[s] year round' and roosts with its mate, using 'thermoregulatory benefits' to bridge cold nights.

traits.skin.note: Feathers: 'a fairly large wren; the second largest in the United States species after the cactus wren'.

traits.flight.note: Powered flight between cover, territory and nest cavities.

traits.metamorphosis.note: None: 'The young hatch' and 'fledge in 12-14 days', so the young are feathered nestlings, not metamorphic larvae.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The nests are arch-shaped structures with a side entrance and built of dried plants or strips of bark', in 'fragmented or complete cavities in trees, or in man-made structures such as bird-boxes, buildings, tin cans, mailboxes': a cavity nest.

traits.perching.note: Perches to sing and roost: males sing from a perch with the tail pointed downward, and pairs 'roost' together for 'thermoregulatory benefits'.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: the validator bands a bird under 0.05 kg as Tiny, and 0.021 kg is well inside that band.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of 'a weight of about 18 to 23 g (0.63 to 0.81 oz)'.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 'a weight of about 18 to 23 g (0.63 to 0.81 oz)'.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 'At 12.5 to 14 cm (4.9 to 5.5 in) long'.

traits.lifespan_y.note: The article gives maximum documented wild ages rather than a mean: 'A male captured in Arkansas lived to be at least 6 years and 1 month old, and in Alabama, the oldest female and male captured were six and ten years old', and 'roughly 90 percent of the banded wrens died within 10 years'. lifespan_y takes 6.0, the lower of the two documented six-year figures, as a conservative documented value rather than an invented mean.

traits.diet.note: 'Their diet consists of invertebrates, such as beetles, true bugs, grasshoppers, katydids, spiders, ants, bees, and wasps. Small lizards and tree frogs also make up the carnivorous portion of their diet. Vegetable matter, such as fruit pulp and various seeds, makes up a small percentage of their diet.' The shares follow that description, with the invertebrate share dominating as the article states and the plant share kept small as it states; the percentages are the author's judgement.

traits.social.note: 'After finding a mate, pairs maintain a territory and stay together for several years' and 'Carolina wrens are both genetically and socially monogamous and will usually mate for life'; group_size covers a pair, its fledged young and, in a feeder, a visiting pair.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'Carolina wrens sing year round and at any point during the daytime, except during the most harsh weather conditions', and it forages by day; the whole behavioural account is diurnal.

traits.defense.note: Mob: 'Both sexes are involved in defending the territory', and in playback experiments 'If the song is not degraded, they respond by attacking', while judging threat size - 'The wrens judge the size of the potential threat, such as a blue jay and avoid the risk of injury when attacking'.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 'it is generally inconspicuous, avoiding the open for extended periods of time. When out in the open, they energetically investigate their surroundings', but it lives 'in suburban yards with abundant thick shrubs' and 'frequent[s]' bird feeders in the north of its range.

habitat.use.note: 'Carolina wrens spend the majority of their time on or near the ground searching for food, or in tangles of vegetation and vines', and 'probe bark crevices on lower tree levels, or pick up leaf-litter in order to search for prey', so ground use dominates while nesting and roosting sit in low cover.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Nests and roosts in cavities, in trees or in man-made structures, 'from 1-3 m from the ground and are rarely higher'.

habitat.resources.note: The invertebrate, small_vertebrate, fruit and seed weights follow the diet shares; cavity is the nest site, shrub_thicket the tangle cover the bird prefers, and leaf_litter the litter it picks through for prey.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: urban_affinity and uses_gardens from 'The preferred habitats are ... suburban yards with abundant thick shrubs and trees, and parks', from 'It has an affinity for dilapidated buildings and unkempt yards in man-made areas', and from the range expansion explanation 'the wrens taking advantage of urban areas containing feeders, especially in winter'; light_max, flight_distance_m and road_mortality are judgement values, the article giving no figures.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'These birds are largely resident, and will only disperse beyond their range after mild winters', so the record is year-round activity.

seasonal.phases.note: The article gives regional egg-laying windows rather than a single one - 'in Texas the time period is from late February to late August, while in Iowa it ranges from late April to June' - and 'As many as three broods may be raised by a pair in a single breeding season'. The breeding window uses the Texas dates, the nearest sourced region to Arkansas, and the day boundaries are the author's judgement; the territorial window covers the stated winter pattern of male-led territory guarding.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'They are incubated by the female for 12-16 days. After the young hatch, they are fed exclusively on invertebrates and fledge in 12-14 days.' duration_days is the upper end of the incubation span plus the fledging span, and scale is a judgement of a recently fledged young bird.

look.note: Plumage from the lead and Description section: a 'fairly large wren' with a strong white supercilium, warm brown upperparts, a pale buffy underside and a barred tail; the record draws a plain warm brown body, a pale eyebrow and underside, a dark barred tail and a dark bill. Proportions are judgement, scaled for a very short-tailed, big-headed, long-legged wren with a fine bill for crevices; the brow and tail_bar parts carry the eyebrow and the barring.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program: invertebrate-led foraging near the ground, a short flee distance for a bird that 'is generally inconspicuous, avoiding the open', and a February-August nest window reflecting up to three broods from a late-February start.
